**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 90, verses 11–20:**

The words of the Most High:

﴿But he has not attempted the ascent.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the ascent is?﴾ ﴿It is freeing a neck,﴾ ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger,﴾ ﴿an orphan near of kin,﴾ ﴿or a needy person in misery.﴾ ﴿Then he is among those who believed and enjoined one another to patience and enjoined one another to compassion.﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of the right.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved in Our signs, they are the companions of the left.﴾ ﴿Over them will be fire, sealed in.﴾

(p-622) The word *al-'Aqabah* (the ascent) in this verse, according to the usage of the Arabs, is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for this deed that is hard on the self, in that it is the expenditure of wealth. It is likened to an *'aqabah* of a mountain, which is the difficult part of it, the part that must be climbed. *Iqtaḥama* means he entered it and passed through it quickly, with pressure and force. As for the exegetes (*mufassirun*, those who interpret the Qur'an), they held that *al-'Aqabah* refers to a mountain in Hell, from which none is saved except by these deeds and the like. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: "*Al-'Aqabah* is Hell." He and Qatadah said: "So storm it through obedience to Allah." And in a hadith: "Indeed, storming it for the believer is like the time between the afternoon prayer and the night prayer."

People differed concerning His words *fa-lā* (then not). The majority of the exegetes said that it is an exhortation (*taḥḍīḍ*) with the meaning of "so why did he not?" Others said it is a supplication, meaning that he deserves to be cursed that he does no good. It was also said that it is a negation, meaning "so he did not storm it." Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj said this, and it is like His words: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [Al-Qiyamah 75:31]. It is pure negation, as if He said: "We gave him the limbs and guided him to the path, yet he did not do any good."

Then Allah the Exalted magnified the matter of the ascent in souls by His words: ﴿And what can make you know what the ascent is?﴾ Then He explained the storming of the ascent by His words: ﴿It is freeing a neck﴾. This is because the implied meaning is: "And what can make you know what the storming of the ascent is?" This is according to the reading of the one who read *fakku raqabatin* (freeing a neck) in the nominative case as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). As for the one who read *fakka* (to free) as a verb and put *raqabah* in the accusative, there is no need to supply "and what can make you know what the storming is." Rather, the magnification applies to the ascent itself, and *fakka* comes as a substitute (*badal*) for *iqtaḥama* and as its explanation.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read: ﴿fakku raqabatin﴾ ﴿aw iṭ'āmun﴾. Abu 'Amr read: "*fakka raqabatan aw aṭ'ama*." Some of the Successors (*tābi'ūn*) read "*fakki raqabatin*" in the genitive. Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr also read "*fakka raqabatin*" in the accusative with "*aw iṭ'āmun*." The arrangement and aspects of these readings are clear.

"*Fakku al-raqabah*" means by freeing from the neck of captivity and slavery. In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever frees a believing soul, Allah will free for each limb of his a limb of his from the Fire."

(p-623) And a Bedouin said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Direct me to a deed by which I may be saved." He said: "If you have shortened the speech, you have indeed asked a big question. Free the neck and free the soul." The Bedouin said: "Are these not one thing?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No. Freeing a soul is that you alone free it, and freeing the neck is that you help with its price."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise is the freeing of a captive, if Allah wills, and his ransom is that the one who ransoms him does it alone. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Bedouin: "And keep ties with the wrongdoing kinsman. If you cannot do all of this, then restrain your tongue except for good."

*Al-Masghabah* means hunger, and *al-sāghib* is the hungry one. Most people read ﴿dhī masghabatin﴾ as a description of "day." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "*dhā masghabatin*," so that it is governed by "*aṭ'ama*" or "*iṭ'ām*" according to the two readings mentioned. In this there is the omission of the described noun (*mawṣūf*) and the placing of the adjective in its position, because the implied meaning is "a person of hunger." The word "*yatīman*" (an orphan) indicates this reading. It is also possible that it is an adjective of His words "*dhā masghabah*" (of hunger). An adjective, when it takes the place of its omitted described noun, resembles nouns. *Al-Masghabah* is general hunger, and it may be used in a specific sense: "*saghiba al-rajul*" means the man became hungry.

His words ﴿dhā maqrabatin﴾ mean "one of near kinship" (*dhū maqrabah*), so that charity and kinship are combined. This is like what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Zaynab, the wife of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Give charity to your husband, for it is for you charity and kinship."

The *aw* (or) in His words ﴿aw miskīnan﴾ carries the meaning of permission and the meaning of option (*takhyīr*), because the speech contains the meaning of urging and command. It also carries the meaning of mere division (*tafṣīl*), because the speech follows the manner of a report, in which *aw* is used only to divide into details. As for the meaning of doubt or ambiguity, it has no place in this verse. Ambiguity is like His words: ﴿Indeed, we or you are upon guidance﴾ [Saba 34:24], and the words of Abu al-Aswad:

*I love Muhammad with a great love, and 'Abbas and Hamzah, or 'Ali.*

*Dhā matrabah* means destitute, one who has clung to the dust. This indicates that the *miskīn* (needy person) is in greater want than the *faqīr* (poor person). Sufyan said: "They are those thrown on the roadside, sitting on the dust, having no houses." Ibn 'Abbas said: "He is the one who goes out of his house, then turns his face back toward his house, certain that there is nothing in it but dust."

His words ﴿Then he was﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿he stormed﴾. The meanings mentioned for ﴿fa-lā iqtaḥama﴾ (so he did not storm), namely negation, exhortation and supplication, apply to it. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' preferred the reading "*fakku raqabatin*" on the basis of His words ﴿Then he was﴾, and the meaning of His words ﴿Then he was﴾ is that he was, at the time of his storming the ascent, among those who believed. The meaning is not that he storms and then afterward becomes a believer, because storming used to occur from a non-believer, and that is of no benefit.

His words ﴿and enjoined one another to patience﴾ mean: to obedience to Allah the Exalted, to His trials and His decree, and to refraining from desires and sins. *Al-Marḥamah* (compassion): Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Everything that leads to the mercy of Allah the Exalted." Others said: it is mutual compassion and the kindness of some people toward others, and in this lies the stability of people; if they did not show compassion at all, they would perish.

*Al-Maymanah* is a place-noun (*maf'alah*) and it is, as is reported, on the right of the Throne. It is the place of Paradise and the station of those among people who are shown mercy. *Al-Mash'amah* is the left-most side, which is the left, and in it is Hell. It is the path of the tormented, who are taken by it to the left. This is derived from Yemen and Syria, for the one standing at the door of the Ka'bah facing the rising of the sun. The left hand is called the *yad al-shu'mā*, and al-Zajjaj and a people held that this is from the concepts of right and left (*yumn* and *shu'm*).

It is possible that one who sees it as from *awṣadtu* may apply hamzah, since the *wāw* is a vowel-letter in the dialect of one who read "*bi'l-sūq*" (with the hamzah). From this is the poet's saying:

*Dear to me are the two who kindle, Musa (with hamzah in both).*

*Mu'ṣadah* is from *āṣadtu*. It is possible to ease the hamzah so that it becomes *mūṣadah* from *āṣadtu*, and from the word *al-waṣīd* (threshold). The poet said:

*A people who treat their children as lice, and chains as shackles, and a door shut tight.*

The exegesis of Surah al-Balad is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
